title: The Journal and the Archive: Buenos Aires, Paris, and the Lacanian Ink Years in New York
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the birth in June
stops.date_confidence: year attested in both Wikipedia editions; the month and day come from the Spanish article alone and are not corroborated anywhere else
stops.campa: Josefina Ayerza is born in Buenos Aires in 1950. The Spanish record gives the first of June; the English record gives only the year, and no source names a hospital, a street, or a parish. She will spend her working life building an archive that dates every seminar and every issue by day and by number. Her own first entry is dated in one language and left bare in the other. Ayerza is an old surname in this city. Whether this Josefina descends from that line, no reachable record says.
suggested_refs: The civil registry of the city of Buenos Aires for June 1950, unconsulted in this pass

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the childhood the record does not keep
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source documents any part of her life in Argentina after the birth entry
stops.campa: Between the birth and the crossing to Paris lie twenty years for which nothing survives: no school, no neighborhood, no first analysis, no account of how a girl in Buenos Aires comes to read Lacan. Argentine psychoanalysis in these decades is the densest in the Americas, and the city talks in its vocabulary at dinner tables. None of the sources place her in any of it. The next attested fact in her life is a move to Paris, and the sources give that one as a decade with no year inside it.
suggested_refs: The Asociacion Psicoanalitica Argentina and the Buenos Aires Lacanian groups of the 1960s, none of which name her

stops.name: Paris, the arrival in the seventies
stops.date_confidence: decade only: both language editions say the 1970s and give no year; the January 1970 stamp is a placeholder, not a finding
stops.campa: She relocates from Buenos Aires to Paris. Both Wikipedia editions say the same eight words and stop: in the 1970s, she relocated to Paris. No year, no arrondissement, no reason, no company. It is the decade in which Lacan's public seminar is at its most crowded and its most contested, the decade after which every institution around it will be dissolved and rebuilt. She arrives in the middle of that weather and the record loses her for ten years. Her next dated appearance anywhere is in 1989, at a workshop she writes up herself.
suggested_refs: French residence and naturalisation records for the 1970s, not consulted

stops.name: Paris, the seminar no source places her inside
stops.date_confidence: unattested: no document of any kind places Ayerza at Lacan's seminar; the stop records the relation, not an attendance
stops.campa: Through these years Jacques Lacan holds his public seminar in Paris, and the transcripts of it will one day be the spine of the website she builds. No document puts her in the room. Her later prose is saturated with the doctrine taught there, she will write in her own voice of her love for Lacan, and she will host his seminars online in their entirety, yet not one source names her as a listener at any session. The connection is textual and it runs backward from New York. Where she actually sat in the 1970s is unrecorded.
suggested_refs: The Faculte de Droit on the Place du Pantheon, where Lacan's seminar met through the 1970s
lacan.com/purloined.htm, her own later hosting of a Lacan seminar text in English

stops.name: Paris, the year the school dissolves
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the dissolution is attested, Ayerza's presence at it is not; inferred from her Paris residence and her later Lacanian affiliations
stops.campa: In January 1980 Lacan dissolves the Ecole Freudienne de Paris by letter, and the analytic city he built breaks into successor schools before the year is out; the Ecole de la Cause freudienne is founded in the same season. Ayerza is in Paris in this period by every account of her movements, and by the 1990s she is a member of the World Association of Psychoanalysis and affiliated to the New Lacanian School, both of them downstream of that break. Where she trained, with whom she analysed, which school took her in: no source says.
suggested_refs: Lacan's letter of dissolution, 5 January 1980, and the founding of the Ecole de la Cause freudienne that followed

stops.name: Paris-New York Psychoanalytic Workshop, the closing address written down
stops.date_confidence: date attested from the piece's own dateline; the source names the workshop and the day and no city at all, so the Paris pin is inference from the workshop's Franco-American form
stops.campa: On the second of April 1989 she writes up Jacques-Alain Miller's closing address to the Paris-New York Psychoanalytic Workshop, and the piece runs under the title Jacques-Alain Miller's Perversion. It is not an interview. It is her account of what he said, in her voice, at the end of a day. The dateline gives the workshop and the date and no place; whether the room was in Paris or in New York the source does not say. She is at this point unpublished as an editor and a year away from founding a journal.
suggested_refs: lacan.com/frameI1.htm, 'Jacques-Alain Miller's Perversion'
sources: lacan.com/frameI1.htm (dateline: Paris-New York Psychoanalytic Workshop, April 2, 1989)

stops.name: Paris, rue Huysmans: the Freudian Field
stops.date_confidence: undated: the membership is attested and career-spanning, the date is a placeholder, and no record places her physically at this address in any year
stops.campa: Her standing biographical note names her a member of the World Association of Psychoanalysis and associates her with the New Lacanian School, the two bodies organised from the Ecole de la Cause freudienne on the rue Huysmans. Membership is attested. Attendance is not: no congress list, no minute, no photograph places her at this address, and the pin follows the institution rather than any recorded visit. Nothing dates her joining either body; the note is written in the present tense and gives no year at all.
suggested_refs: The Ecole de la Cause freudienne, 1 rue Huysmans, Paris, seat of the Association Mondiale de Psychanalyse

stops.name: Manhattan, the arrival with no date
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source dates the move from Paris to New York; 1985 is arithmetic on the gap between the attested 1970s Paris residence and the attested 1990 founding
stops.campa: Somewhere in the 1980s she crosses again, Paris to New York, and the sources do not record it. The English entry runs the two facts together in a single line: Paris in the 1970s, Lacanian Ink in New York in 1990. Between them sits a whole move, an apartment, a practice opened, a working language changed for the second time. The date placed on this stop is arithmetic on that gap. She holds Argentine and American citizenship, which fixes the arrival only as somewhere before a naturalisation nobody has dated.
suggested_refs: United States naturalisation records, not consulted

stops.name: Manhattan, Lacanian Ink founded
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month, day, or launch address in any source
stops.campa: In 1990 she founds Lacanian Ink, a journal that puts psychoanalysis at the same table as contemporary art and philosophy and refuses to keep the three apart. She writes the editorials herself. No launch address survives, no first-issue party, no masthead photograph: the journal simply exists from 1990 and does not stop. Richard Kostelanetz will later count it among the few cultural journals of its founding moment still running, alongside Bomb. His comparison is relayed here at second hand; the underlying text was not located.
suggested_refs: Lacanian Ink, issue 1 (1990), not located in this pass

stops.name: Manhattan, Zizek on the masthead from the first issue
stops.date_confidence: attested as from the journal's founding; no month given, the June stamp is a placeholder inside the founding year
stops.campa: Slavoj Zizek joins the editorial board at the founding and stays on it. The journal begins running early drafts of his books in English before the books exist, so that through the 1990s Lacanian Ink becomes one of the first places an American reader meets him at all. She interviews him, publishes him, launches issues with him reading aloud in downtown galleries, and keeps his essays on a server she maintains herself. He will call her the indefatigable operator of what he considers the best Lacanian website in existence.
suggested_refs: The Lacanian Ink masthead, 1990 onward

stops.name: White Street, Tribeca: the development of THE THING
stops.date_confidence: year attested from her own photo caption; no month, and the caption does not say how many times she was there
stops.campa: The year is 1994 and the meetings are at Wolfgang Staehle's studio on White Street in Tribeca, where THE THING is being developed: an artists' bulletin board system, one of the first places downtown New York talks to itself over a wire. Her own caption records the address, the year, and community building. Whether she co-founds anything here is not established, and Staehle's project predates the meeting by three years. What is established is that she is in the room while a network is being made, three years before she builds one.
suggested_refs: THE THING BBS, founded by Wolfgang Staehle c.1991
sources: lacan.com/josefinaslide/ (caption: Wolfgang Staehle's studio, Tribeca, White St., NYC, 1994)

stops.name: Deutsches Haus, Columbia University: More Hysteria, Please
stops.date_confidence: season attested as winter 1995; the exact day is not given, and the December stamp is a placeholder
stops.campa: In the winter of 1995 she sits with the theatre director Richard Foreman at Deutsches Haus on the Columbia campus, in front of an audience, and the two negotiate on the spot what kind of exchange this is going to be. An analytic session slides into an interview and slides back. Neither of them settles it. A journal that will not decide whether talk with an artist is criticism or clinic has no need to settle it either. The transcript runs in Lacanian Ink 11 under the title More Hysteria, Please.
suggested_refs: Lacanian Ink 11, 'More Hysteria, Please'

stops.name: Manhattan, lacan.com built
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month, and no source describes the circumstances of the build
stops.campa: In 1997 she builds lacan.com. Onto it go Jacques Lacan's own seminars, in full, alongside Slavoj Zizek, Alain Badiou and Jacques-Alain Miller, plus bibliographies of living artists. It is an archive with no institution behind it, no library, no grant named in any source, run by an analyst with a private practice and a journal. Somewhere in that web the English Seminar on The Purloined Letter sits at lacan.com/purloined.htm, quoted as a primary text by readers who never learn whose server it is on.
suggested_refs: lacan.com/lacan1.htm, the site index and its History section

stops.name: New Museum, 583 Broadway: photographed with Zizek
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by her own caption; the coordinate is the museum's SoHo address, which two entries in the research pool give slightly differently
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of October 1999 she is photographed with Slavoj Zizek at the New Museum of Contemporary Art, in the old building on Broadway in SoHo, eight years before the museum moves to the Bowery. It is the year she begins staging philosophers in rooms built for looking at art rather than in lecture halls: the Drawing Center, this museum, Deitch, Tilton. Her caption for the photograph dates it to the day and calls the place, twice in one line, the old one.
stops.quote: With Slavoj Zizek at the New Museum, in the old days, in the old building, October 14, 1999
suggested_refs: The New Museum of Contemporary Art at 583 Broadway, its home from 1983 to 2007

stops.name: The Drawing Center, Wooster Street: the series begins
stops.date_confidence: start year attested; the individual evenings inside the series are undated in every source, and the Drawing Center is given here as one named venue of four
stops.campa: From 1999 she runs a series of cultural events pairing international philosophers with galleries: the Drawing Center on Wooster Street, the New Museum, Deitch Projects, the Tilton Gallery. No source dates the individual evenings inside the series. The surviving photographs show an editor booking the philosophers she publishes into the rooms she writes about, on the same island, for the better part of a decade. Which of the four venues took the first evening, and who spoke at it, is not recorded anywhere the site still serves.
suggested_refs: The Drawing Center, 35 Wooster Street, SoHo
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Josefina Ayerza' (names the four venues without dating individual events)

stops.name: Manhattan, Badiou joins the board
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month given
stops.campa: In 2000 Alain Badiou joins the editorial board of Lacanian Ink, writing on Lacanian theory and the Marxist tradition. With Zizek there since the founding, the journal now carries two of the philosophers whose English-language reception it is in the middle of building. Badiou is not at this date widely translated. No month is given for the appointment, only the year. He will read at three of the journal's launches over the following seven years, twice in a SoHo gallery and once uptown.
suggested_refs: The Lacanian Ink editorial board, 2000 onward

stops.name: Deitch Projects, SoHo: Lacanian Ink 17 on aesthetics
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the caption says West Broadway while Deitch's principal SoHo space in these years is on Wooster Street, and the discrepancy is left standing
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of November 2000 the seventeenth issue of Lacanian Ink launches at Deitch Projects, the issue given over to aesthetics. Ayerza introduces and runs the discussion. The caption gives the gallery's street as West Broadway, though Deitch's principal SoHo space through these years is on Wooster Street, and neither reading is set aside for the other. Alain Badiou reads a paper called Art and Philosophy and then, the caption records, recites Mallarme to the room.
suggested_refs: Lacanian Ink 17, on aesthetics
Deitch Projects, SoHo, 1996-2010
sources: lacan.com/josefinaslide/ (caption: Deitch Projects, West Broadway, NYC, November 30, 2000)

stops.name: Jack Tilton Gallery, Greene Street: Lacanian Ink 19
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the caption gives only the gallery and SoHo, and the Greene Street coordinate comes from the gallery's own documented 1993-2005 address
stops.campa: Two months after the towers come down, on the fourteenth of November 2001, the nineteenth issue launches at the Jack Tilton Gallery in SoHo and Slavoj Zizek speaks on Passions of the Real. The phrase will carry into the book he writes in New York that winter. Ayerza introduces the papers and takes the discussion. The caption names no street. Tilton had moved the gallery to Greene Street in 1993 and stays there until 2005, and the pin follows that address.
suggested_refs: Lacanian Ink 19
Slavoj Zizek, Welcome to the Desert of the Real (2002)

stops.name: Deitch Projects, SoHo: the double issue on eroticism
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the caption; the caption gives no street number, so the pin follows Deitch's main space at 18 Wooster Street rather than any address in the source
stops.campa: On the first of April 2005 the double issue 24/25, on eroticism, launches at Deitch Projects. Badiou reads The Subject of Art; the analyst Stuart Schneiderman and the critic Adrian Dannatt are in the room. It is the second launch Badiou reads at, four and a half years after the first. Her slideshow keeps the date, the venue and the programme, no street number and not one word about what was said afterward. The pin follows Deitch's main space on Wooster Street, which the caption does not name.
suggested_refs: Lacanian Ink 24/25, on eroticism
Alain Badiou, 'The Subject of Art'

stops.name: Pratt Institute, Brooklyn: the opening paper
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by her own caption
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of November 2006 she crosses the river to Pratt Institute in Brooklyn, invited by Alain Badiou to open the proceedings with a paper of her own. Her caption for the photograph says only that. Badiou, six years on her editorial board by now, is the host here and she is the one being listened to, which happens in almost none of the other pictures. The title of the paper is not recorded at any address the site still serves, and no programme for the day was found.
stops.quote: I was invited by Alain Badiou to read an opening paper.
suggested_refs: Pratt Institute, Brooklyn, November 2006

stops.name: Jack Tilton Gallery, East 76th Street: uptown with Badiou
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the caption
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of November 2007 she appears with Alain Badiou at the Tilton Gallery again, now uptown at 8 East 76th Street, the gallery having left SoHo two years earlier. It is the same pairing and the same week of the year as the 2001 evening downtown, in a different half of the city. The caption gives the day, the gallery and the pairing, and attaches no issue number to the evening. Deitch will close in 2010 and the run of launches in dealers' front rooms ends with the decade. Badiou by this date is translated and widely read.
suggested_refs: Jack Tilton Gallery, 8 East 76th Street, its address from 2005

stops.name: David Zwirner Gallery, West 19th Street: dated by a reflection
stops.date_confidence: undated in the caption; the photograph can only be bracketed as after 2007, from the completed IAC building reflected in the gallery glass, and the 2008 stamp is the earliest year that bracket allows
stops.campa: Gerard Wajcman photographs her arriving at David Zwirner's Chelsea gallery, where she has arranged to meet him. The caption carries no year. Frank Gehry's IAC building stands reflected in the gallery's glass, and that building was not finished before 2007, which puts the photograph after it. Zwirner had left SoHo for West 19th Street in 2002. Between those two facts, and no others, the picture sits somewhere in the last years the journal was launching issues in rooms.
suggested_refs: The IAC Building, 555 West 18th Street, completed 2007, visible in the caption's reflection

stops.name: SoHo, the twenty-third of April: two captions, one evening
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested twice over; the venue and the issue number are attested in two mutually exclusive versions and the contradiction is unresolved
stops.campa: Two captions on her own slideshow give the same date, the twenty-third of April 2009, to two different events at two different galleries: the launch of Lacanian Ink 33 at Jack Tilton, and the launch of Lacanian Ink 23 at Deitch. Both cannot be right, and the two issue numbers are years apart in the journal's own run. The site does not resolve it. The pin sits in SoHo, between the two claimed rooms. Which of them she was standing in that night, the archive does not say, and nothing else reachable says it either.
suggested_refs: Lacanian Ink 23 and Lacanian Ink 33, both claimed as launching on 23 April 2009

stops.name: Cadaques, the summer she keeps returning to
stops.date_confidence: undated: neither the events recalled nor the essay recording them carries a year in any reachable source, and the placement in this sequence is editorial
stops.campa: On the Costa Brava, in the town where Dali kept his house, she meets the photographer Alex Kayser. She writes it down years afterward in the first person, for an issue of The Symptom, under a title that admits a habit rather than an occasion: When I Come to Cadaques I Always Stay Here. The essay is the only sustained autobiographical prose of hers that any source reaches. In it there is no sand, only stones, and the man with the camera around his neck is very tall.
stops.quote: The place was in fact very nice, the Mediterranean blue as ever, the stones, oh well, no sand, we loved, enjoyed every part of it.
stops.quote_source: Josefina Ayerza, 'When I Come to Cadaques I Always Stay Here', The Symptom 18, lacan.com/symptom/alex-kayser/
suggested_refs: The Symptom, issue 18, the last issue of the web journal, Fall 2019

stops.name: Cadaques, the question about Alien
stops.date_confidence: undated: the anecdote sits inside the same undated essay and carries no year of its own
stops.campa: In the same memoir she is introduced to a Swiss artist and hears herself ask whether he is the one who did Alien. She reports the sentence exactly as it left her, hesitation and all, in a journal she edits and could have tidied at any point. Cadaques in these years is that kind of town: Dali down the road, photographers on the terraces, a designer of monsters, everybody summering in the same few streets above the same stony water. She does not say what year it is and the issue listing does not date the essay.
stops.quote: You are…Hans Giger, who did Alien?
stops.quote_source: Josefina Ayerza, 'When I Come to Cadaques I Always Stay Here', The Symptom 18, lacan.com/symptom/alex-kayser/
suggested_refs: H. R. Giger's summers on the Costa Brava, undocumented in the sources consulted

stops.name: Cadaques, the body given in parts
stops.date_confidence: undated: the essay is undated, and the Lacanian Ink issue carrying Kayser's photographs of her is not identified by number in the testimonial that praises it
stops.campa: Kayser photographs bodies in fragments, a hand, a shoulder, a back, and she recognises the procedure at once: it is what Jacques Lacan's teaching had already trained her to see, the body given as pieces before it is given whole. Later, photographs he took of her in Cadaques run in an issue of Lacanian Ink, and Pierre-Gilles Gueguen writes in to praise them, naming her as the sitter and Kayser as the eye. Adrian Dannatt, on the same page, writes about the Dali pictures of Dali and of her.
stops.quote: Because of my love for Jacques Lacan I was promptly taken by the way Alex would focus on body parts.
stops.quote_source: Josefina Ayerza, 'When I Come to Cadaques I Always Stay Here', The Symptom 18, lacan.com/symptom/alex-kayser/
suggested_refs: Pierre-Gilles Gueguen's and Adrian Dannatt's testimonials at lacan.com/lacan1.htm
sources: lacan.com/lacan1.htm (Gueguen: 'ones taken of you by Alex Kayser in our beloved Cadaques')

stops.name: Manhattan, a book called Voyeurism
stops.date_confidence: year attested in one bibliography only; no publisher, no month, no copy located
stops.campa: In 2002 she publishes a book called Voyeurism. The Spanish bibliography lists it and nothing else does: no publisher reachable, no page count, no review. The title is one word, from an editor who has by then spent a decade putting analysts into galleries and photographers into a psychoanalytic journal. What is inside the book is not established anywhere, and no copy of it was located in this pass. Not even the language it was written in is recorded. The entry gives the year and stops.
suggested_refs: Josefina Ayerza, Voyeurism (2002), unlocated

stops.name: Manhattan, Comme des Garcons
stops.date_confidence: undated: the essay carries no year on the page that hosts it and the issue is not numbered in the reachable listing
stops.campa: Her essay Comme des Garcons opens with a question rather than a claim: what is castration in this context. It runs in Lacanian Ink and moves between clothes, Lacan's twentieth seminar, and Saint Teresa in her marble ecstasy, asking whether the saint's being emptied out conveys the flavour of what happens in analysis. The woman of the seminar walks through the essay in a not-whole, non-existent apparel. It is criticism written in the vocabulary of the clinic, with no translation offered to a reader who lacks it.
stops.quote: If symptom is the single way each one happens to enjoy his/her unconscious framework, symptom is as well what you structure your life around.
suggested_refs: Lacan, Seminar XX (Encore), the reference running under the essay

stops.name: Manhattan, the interviews with no dates
stops.date_confidence: undated: her own bibliography lists these interviews without years or locations, and the 2004 stamp is a placeholder for the whole run of them
stops.campa: Across the journal's decades she interviews the people she publishes and the people she looks at: Matthew Barney, Shirin Neshat, Catherine Opie, Julia Kristeva, Richard Rorty. Not one of the interviews carries a date in the bibliography her own site keeps, and not one names a location. They were done somewhere, over some years, by an analyst asking artists questions in the register she uses in the consulting room. What the page records is that they exist.
suggested_refs: lacan.com/JosArt.htm, her own article and interview bibliography

stops.name: Manhattan, sitting Zizek down
stops.date_confidence: undated in the bibliography, like the rest of the interviews; the placeholder year falls in the middle of their working relationship, not on any recorded day
stops.campa: She interviews Slavoj Zizek and publishes it. He has been on her masthead since the founding, in her issues in draft before he is in print anywhere, on her server in essay and in video, reading aloud at her launches in two SoHo galleries. Somewhere inside that traffic she sits him down and asks the questions herself. The bibliography lists the piece without a date, like everything else on that page. Which issue carried it is not stated there, and no other listing supplies it.
suggested_refs: lacan.com/JosArt.htm, interview listing
sources: lacan.com (Zizek's published praise of the site)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Planning Stages
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the article is listed without a dateline, and no source establishes whether she travelled to Buenos Aires for it or reported it from New York
stops.campa: She writes a profile of the painter Guillermo Kuitca for Artforum under the title Planning Stages, on a compatriot who paints beds and maps and floor plans of buildings nobody lives in. Whether the piece took her back to his Buenos Aires studio or was made in New York from photographs and a telephone is stated by no source found. The pin sits on the city the two of them were born in. Her own bibliography lists the article with no dateline and no year.
suggested_refs: Josefina Ayerza, 'Planning Stages: Guillermo Kuitca', Artforum

stops.name: Manhattan, the criticism circuit
stops.date_confidence: career-spanning and undated: the magazines are attested, the individual pieces are not dated in any recoverable bibliography
stops.campa: Her standing biography lists the magazines: Artforum, Flash Art, Du in Zurich, L'Ane in Paris, and Lacanian Ink, which is her own. She writes on Wolfgang Tillmans, Gregory Crewdson, Juliana Huxtable. One piece for Le Nouvel Ane carries a title that is the whole argument of her New York decades in six words: A New York, l'art traite le dechet. No dated bibliography of the individual articles was recoverable, and Artforum's own contributor archive returned a paywall when asked.
suggested_refs: Josefina Ayerza, 'A New York, l'art traite le dechet', Le Nouvel Ane 9

stops.name: Manhattan, Contagious
stops.date_confidence: undated in the listing; the swine flu in the title brackets it loosely to 2009 or after, and nothing in the source confirms even that
stops.campa: Two more pieces from the same bibliography, both undated: an essay on Cy Twombly for Hurly-Burly, and one for the Lacanian Compass called Contagious: Swine Flu, Suicide, Hysteria, which sets an epidemic, an act and a diagnosis in one line and lets them argue among themselves. The influenza in the title brackets that piece loosely to 2009 or later. Nothing in the source confirms even that much, and the Twombly essay carries no bracket at all. Neither piece names a place of writing.
suggested_refs: Lacanian Compass 14, 'Contagious: Swine Flu, Suicide, Hysteria'
Hurly-Burly, the essay on Cy Twombly

stops.name: Manhattan, the practice with no address
stops.date_confidence: career-spanning and undated: the practice is attested with no start date and no address in any source, and the stamp is a placeholder in the middle of its run
stops.campa: Under all of it, from before the journal and still, there is a private psychoanalytic practice in New York City: patients, hours, a couch, a door. No address is given by any source. It is the only part of her working life that leaves no bibliography, no slideshow, no launch photograph. Her own bios line calls her a psychoanalyst before it calls her anything else, and names the World Association of Psychoanalysis in the same breath. That is the whole of what the record says about the clinic.
stops.quote: JOSEFINA AYERZA is a psychoanalyst, member of the WAP - World Association of Psychoanalysis. and has a private practice in New York City.
suggested_refs: The World Association of Psychoanalysis membership rolls, not consulted

stops.name: New Museum, 235 Bowery: the same door, eleven years on
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested by the caption; no day given
stops.campa: In January 2010 Pierre-Gilles Gueguen photographs her standing against the door of the New Museum's new building on the Bowery, the museum having left Broadway in 2007. Eleven years earlier she had been photographed at the old address on Broadway with Slavoj Zizek beside her, and the caption for that one insisted on saying so twice. The two pictures are kept in the same slideshow, one after the other, an editor filing her own life the way she files an issue: by venue, by date, with the change of address noted. Gueguen, who takes this one, is the same analyst who once wrote in to praise photographs of her taken in Cadaques.
suggested_refs: The New Museum's Bowery building, opened December 2007

stops.name: A studio in Manhattan, Visions of the Couch
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the posting date on the journal's blog
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of July 2010 four photographs run under her name on the journal's blog. They are of a couch, in her New York studio, taken by a photographer credited only as KiNo. There is no accompanying text: no essay, no caption, not a line of the vocabulary she has used on every other page of the site. Four images of the analytic couch and nothing else, published by a woman who has spent twenty years in print explaining what happens on one. The studio's address is not given, then or anywhere.
suggested_refs: lacan.com/journal9/?p=520, 'Visions of the Couch'

stops.name: Manhattan, the thirty-seventh issue
stops.date_confidence: year attested in one bibliography only; no month, no theme recorded
stops.campa: In 2011 she edits and publishes the thirty-seventh issue of Lacanian Ink, twenty-one years after the first. The Spanish bibliography lists it by number and gives it no theme. By this point the journal has outlived most of the galleries that launched its issues: Deitch closes in 2010, Tilton has moved twice and left SoHo for good, the New Museum is in its second building and its second neighbourhood. The launches with philosophers reading aloud in a dealer's front room belong to a decade that has ended. She is sixty-one and still writing the editorials herself.
suggested_refs: Lacanian Ink 37 (2011)

stops.name: SoHo, the lychee martini
stops.date_confidence: undated: the caption gives neither year nor the name of the restaurant, and the placement here is editorial
stops.campa: A photograph in the slideshow, undated: Ayerza and Victoria Bullrich at a Korean restaurant in SoHo, drinking lychee martinis. Bullrich is another Buenos Aires surname and the caption says nothing about how the two women know each other; no other source mentions her at all. Ayerza filed the picture among the launches and the philosophers, on the same slideshow and with the same weight. The caption names the two women and the drink and nothing else. The restaurant is not named and the year is gone.
